chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from Ali ibn Asbat from Muhammad ibn Ziyad from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'A man gave his wife the option of divorce (khul' or tawliq), and he said: "The choice is hers only as long as they remain in their session; when they separate, she has no choice." I said to him, 'May God improve you, but if she divorces herself three times before they separate from their session?' He said, 'It will not be more than one [divorce], and he has more right to take her back before her waiting period expires, for the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) gave his wives the choice, and they chose him, so that was a [revocable] divorce.' He said, 'And I said to him, "What if they chose themselves?"' He said to me, 'What do you think of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) if they chose themselves, would he keep them?'

key_terms.الْخِيَار: The option/choice (specifically tawliq, giving the wife the power to divorce herself)
key_terms.رَجْعَتِهَا: Taking her back (the husband's right to resume marriage during the waiting period without a new contract)
key_terms.طَلَقًا: Divorce (specifically implying a revocable divorce in this context)
key_terms.مَجْلِسِهِمَا: Their session (the time period during which the option remains valid)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal effect if a wife exercises her option of divorce multiple times in one session?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Baqir clarifies the mechanics of conditional divorce (tawliq), establishing that multiple self-divorces within the same session count as a single revocable divorce (talaq raj'i), preserving the husband's right of return. The Imam reinforces this by citing the precedent of the Prophet’s wives, whose choice to remain with him was treated as a definitive act, thereby illustrating the legal weight of such decisions in Shia jurisprudence.
